title: Authorization and Row Level Security
summary: Logging in says who you are. Authorization decides what you may touch. Here is how Supabase Row Level Security makes the database enforce it, row by row.
youWillLearn: Why a check in the browser is not a check
How to write Supabase RLS policies with using and with check
The three common ways RLS gets skipped, and how to test it

glossary.authorization: Deciding what a known user may see or change. It comes after authentication, which only proves who they are.
glossary.authentication: Proving who you are, for example with a password or Sign in with Google.
glossary.Data API: The web API Supabase puts in front of your Postgres tables, so browser code can query them with the anon key and the user's token.
glossary.Row Level Security: A Postgres feature that filters every query row by row, using rules you attach to the table. Called RLS for short.
glossary.policy: One RLS rule on a table: for which action (select, insert, update, delete), for which users, and which rows pass.
glossary.auth.uid(): A Supabase SQL function that returns the logged-in user's id, read from the verified JWT sent with the request.
glossary.default deny: When RLS is on and no policy allows something, it is refused. Nothing is visible until you say so.
glossary.with check: The part of a policy that tests the new version of a row on insert or update, so users cannot write rows they should not own.
glossary.service role key: A Supabase key that skips RLS entirely. It is for trusted server code only, never the browser.
glossary.view: A saved query that looks like a table. In Postgres it runs with its creator's rights by default, which can skip RLS.

steps.title: Logged in is not the same as allowed
body: Notely's browser code asks Supabase for notes: from('notes').select('*'). Maya is logged in, so the request carries her token.
The answer: every note from every user. Logging in proved who Maya is. Nothing yet decides which rows she may see.

scene.caption: Maya asks for notes and gets everyone's. Nothing filters the rows.

steps.title: Who you are vs what you may do
body: Two separate questions. Authentication: who are you? The last two lessons answered that. Authorization: now that we know, what may you touch?
For Notely the rule is short: Maya sees and edits her own notes, nobody else's. The job is to make that rule impossible to skip.

callout.text: At a hotel, the front desk checks your ID once: authentication. Your key card then opens room 214 and nothing else: authorization.

scene.caption: Maya's identity is known. The missing piece is a rule about which rows are hers.

steps.title: A check in the browser is not a check
body: Filtering Ben's notes out in React only hides them. Anyone can open DevTools, take their own token, and query the API directly.
With Supabase, the browser talks straight to the database through the Data API. So the database itself has to enforce the rule. That is Row Level Security, or RLS.

callout.text: The same goes for your own API routes. The server decides what each user may do. The UI only reflects that decision.

scene.caption: Anyone can skip your UI and call the API directly. The rule must live in the database.

steps.title: Turn RLS on: everything locks
body: One line switches RLS on for a table. From then on, every query from the browser is filtered by rules called policies.
With RLS on and no policies, users get zero rows. That is default deny: nothing is visible until a policy allows it. A safe starting point.

code.code: alter table notes enable row level security;

scene.caption: RLS is on and there are no policies yet. Every request gets an empty list.

steps.title: A policy: only your own rows
body: A policy says which rows pass. auth.uid() returns the user id from the verified JWT you met in lesson 02. Postgres compares it with each row's user_id.
This happens inside the database, on every query, whatever the browser asked for. Maya gets her 12 notes. A select * from DevTools gets the same 12.

code.code:
create policy "read own notes"
on notes for select
to authenticated
using ( (select auth.uid()) = user_id );
code.caption: Wrapping auth.uid() in (select …) lets Postgres compute it once per query, not once per row.

scene.caption: The policy filters rows inside the database. Maya gets exactly her own notes.

steps.title: Writes need with check
body: using decides which existing rows you can see or touch. with check tests the row you are about to write.
Without it, Maya could insert a note with user_id set to Ben's id, or move her own note into his account. Inserts need with check. Updates need both parts.

scene.caption: A write with someone else's user_id fails the with check test.

steps.title: Sharing a note with Ben
body: Maya wants Ben to read one note. Notely adds a note_shares table: which note, shared with whom.
The read policy now lets a row through if you own it or a share row points at you. Still one rule in the database, so every screen and every API call obeys it.

code.caption: This replaces "read own notes". note_shares needs RLS too, with a policy letting users read shares that involve them: the subquery obeys it.

scene.caption: Ben sees the one note Maya shared, because a share row points at him.

steps.title: Three ways RLS gets skipped
body: 1. The service role key ignores RLS completely. Fine in trusted server code, a disaster if it reaches the browser (next lesson).
2. A view runs with its creator's rights unless you create it with (security_invoker = true).
3. Tables created with SQL, including Claude Code's migrations, start with RLS off. One forgotten migration line and the table is open to anyone with the anon key.

callout.text: Never base a policy on user_metadata in the JWT. Users can edit their own metadata. Use a table you control, or app_metadata, which only the server can set.

scene.caption: Server code with the service role key goes straight past the policy.

steps.title: Test it as two different users
body: Do not trust a policy because it reads well. Log in as Maya, then as Ben, and try to read, edit and delete each other's notes. Every attempt should fail or return nothing.
Then list every table and check that RLS is on for each one. Supabase's Security Advisor in the dashboard flags open tables too.

code.code:
select tablename, rowsecurity
from pg_tables
where schemaname = 'public'
order by rowsecurity, tablename;
code.caption: Any row with rowsecurity = false is likely open to anyone with the anon key, for reads and writes.

callout.text: After Claude Code adds a table, ask: is RLS enabled in the same migration? Which policies exist for select, insert, update and delete? Does every insert and update policy have with check? Is the service role key used anywhere a user's request can reach?

scene.caption: Two accounts, same query, different answers. That is what a working policy looks like.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Authentication says who you are. Authorization says what you may touch, and it must live where nobody can skip it. With Supabase that is the database: turn RLS on for every table, write a policy per action with auth.uid(), add with check on writes.
Keep the service role key on the server, and test with two real accounts.

quiz.question: Claude Code built a Notely dashboard that hides other users' notes with a .filter() in React. RLS is off. Is the data safe?

options.text: Yes, because users only see what the UI shows.
options.why: The UI is not the only way in. Anyone can call the Supabase API from DevTools with their own token and read every row.

options.text: No. Turn on RLS and add policies so the database filters the rows.
options.why: Authorization must happen where the user cannot skip it. With Supabase, that is RLS in the database.

options.text: Yes, as long as the anon key stays secret.
options.why: The anon key is meant to be in the browser, so it is not a secret. RLS is what makes it safe to publish.

quiz.question: A table has RLS enabled and a select policy, but no other policies. What happens when Maya tries to insert a row from the browser?

options.text: It succeeds, because she is logged in.
options.why: Being logged in is authentication. With RLS on, an action without a matching policy is refused.

options.text: It succeeds, but only for her own rows.
options.why: No insert policy means no rule saying which rows are hers to insert, so nothing passes.

options.text: It fails. With no insert policy, inserts are denied.
options.why: RLS is default deny. Each action needs its own policy, and writes need with check.

quiz.question: Notely adds an admin page. Which of these policy checks could a regular user cheat to get admin rights?

options.why: Users can update their own user_metadata, so they can give themselves any role. Base roles on app_metadata or a table only the server writes.

options.text: One that checks a roles table that only server code can write.
options.why: This is the safe pattern. Users cannot change a table they have no write policy on.
This only matches rows the user owns. It does not hand out any role.

takeaways: Authentication is who you are. Authorization is what you may touch. Logging in does not answer the second question.
Checks in the browser only hide data. Enforce rules on the server, or with Supabase, in the database with RLS.
Turn RLS on in the same migration that creates the table, then write a policy per action using (select auth.uid()).
Insert and update policies need with check, or users can write rows that belong to someone else.
The service role key, views without security_invoker, and user_metadata are the classic holes. Test with two accounts.
